blocks.content: The Continental Drift Theory was proposed by Alfred Wegener in 1912. According to this theory, the present continents were once part of a single massive landform that gradually fragmented and drifted apart.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Alfred Wegener proposed the Continental Drift Theory in 1912 regarding the distribution of oceans and continents.
All landmasses initially formed a single supercontinent called Pangaea, surrounded by the mega-ocean Panthalassa.
Pangaea split into Laurasia (northern block) and Gondwanaland (southern block) separated by the Tethys Sea.
Major supporting evidence includes the Jig-Saw Fit of shorelines, tillite sedimentary deposits, and identical fossil distributions across distant oceans.
The theory faced criticism because proposed mechanisms like polar-fleeing force and tidal force were deemed inadequate.

cells: A supercontinent that existed about 300 million years ago during the late Paleozoic era.
The vast global ocean that surrounded Pangaea.

blocks.content: • Around 200 million years ago, Pangaea began to break apart due to internal forces.
• It first divided into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south.
All the continents formed a single continental mass and a mega-ocean surrounded the same.
• Subsequent fragmentation produced the present continents.
• The Atlantic Ocean formed as the Americas drifted away from Europe and Africa.

rows: South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica

blocks.content: • Jigsaw Fit: The coastlines of South America and Africa match remarkably well.
• Fossil Evidence: Fossils of Mesosaurus, Glossopteris, and Lystrosaurus are found on continents now separated by oceans.
• Geological Similarity: Mountain ranges such as the Appalachians align with those in Scotland and Scandinavia.
• Paleoclimatic Evidence: Glacial deposits in India, Africa, and Australia indicate they were once near the South Pole.
• Mineral Distribution: Similar mineral belts occur across different continents.

items: Gondwanaland landmasses included modern-day South America, Africa, Madagascar, India, Australia, and Antarctica.
Distribution of Mesosaurus fossils in South Africa and Brazil is a frequently tested piece of evidence.
Wegener suggested pole-fleeing force (rotation of Earth) and tidal force (moon/sun attraction) as forces responsible for drift.

blocks.content: • Wegener could not identify the exact force responsible for continental movement.
• He proposed tidal forces and pole-fleeing forces, which were too weak.
• The idea that continents plowed through ocean crust was scientifically incorrect.
